questions.title: What is Online Reputation Monitoring & Brand Mention Tracking?
questions.answer: Online Reputation Monitoring & Brand Mention Tracking — also called online brand monitoring or internet reputation monitoring — is a full-program retainer for enterprise reputation monitoring and media monitoring services: ongoing, real-time monitoring of everything published about you across media, social, search, reviews and AI-generated answers, read by analysts who separate signal from noise and escalate confirmed risk to a team — not a self-serve listening dashboard.

questions.title: How is this different from Control (SERM) or Crisis Management (Defence)?
questions.answer: Continuous Monitoring only watches and signals — it doesn't change your search results (that's RH Control) and it doesn't fight an active crisis (that's RH Defence). Think of it as the layer that tells you when either of those is needed, before it becomes obvious to everyone else.

questions.title: What's included in the five RCC modules?
questions.answer: As part of our reputation monitoring services: search results (SERP), social & mention listening (SCAN), AI answer tracking, reviews & ratings, and sentiment/tone — all five run together as one contour, with a shared RPN risk score and alerting on top.

questions.title: Does this include AI assistants like ChatGPT and Gemini?
questions.answer: Yes. AI Representation Analysis tracks how ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok and Perplexity answer real questions about you, scored on relevance, volume and how clean of negative framing the answer came back.

questions.title: How is pricing structured?
questions.answer: A monthly retainer, $5–25K/month, depending on the scope of your field, languages and regions. Full tiers are on the pricing page, or a confidential audit confirms the exact quote.

questions.title: Is this online media monitoring, or does it cover offline channels too?
questions.answer: This is online brand surveillance and monitoring — media, social, search, reviews and AI answers across digital channels. Broadcast and print aren't covered; if a story breaks there, it almost always surfaces online within hours, and that's where the platform picks it up.

questions.title: Is this a media tracking service, or software I run myself?
questions.answer: It's a media tracking service, not self-serve software. You get full platform access to Risk Control Center, but a dedicated analyst team reads the field every day and escalates confirmed risk — the software alone is what a SaaS monitoring tool sells you.

questions.title: How much media mentions tracking is actually included — every single mention?
questions.answer: Media mentions tracking runs across your entire field — media, social, search, reviews and AI answers — but analysts filter signal from noise first. You're not handed a raw feed of every mention; you see the ones that are actually risk, scored and prioritized.

questions.title: Is this suitable for compliance teams, or just PR/comms?

For General Counsel and compliance leads, this runs as online brand compliance monitoring — negative-news screening built into ongoing coverage, not a one-off check before a deal. Any media monitoring organization, from a single enterprise brand to a multi-brand holding, gets the same one-score view.

sections.title: What is Social Listening? Quick Definition
body: Social listening is tracking what people say about your brand across social platforms, forums, blogs, video and press, then reading it for tone and risk — not just counting how many times you were mentioned. Social monitoring is the narrower version of that: watching a channel for volume and alerts. Most brands actually want something in between: a social listening platform that also has someone reading it. Whatever you call the category: social listening software or social media monitoring software — that's the version this page describes.

questions.answer: Monitoring usually means watching one channel for volume and basic alerts. What runs on this retainer combines both: full-channel coverage plus a human who actually reads it.

Mass discount codes can drive most of the growth in mentions, while a handful of niche organic placements deliver disproportionately higher engagement per mention.

sections.title: Signs your brand requires AI reputation monitoring

cards.title: The Sign
parts: ChatGPT gets asked about you, and nobody at your company sees the answer. A customer, investor or candidate asks an AI-powered assistant about your company — the answer could be accurate, outdated or unflattering, and right now you have no way of knowing which.
Why it matters

AI answers are becoming the first impression. For a growing share of buyers, investors and candidates, that answer is the only account of your company they see before they decide. It carries your brand's voice whether you wrote a word of it or not — shaping brand reputation before you know it happened.

cards.title: The Sign
parts: No one owns this yet. SEO owns Google. PR owns the media. Marketing owns the campaigns. Nobody’s job description says "watch what ChatGPT says about us" — so it sits unmanaged in the gap between teams.
Why it matters

The model recommends — someone has to know what it’s recommending. Ask an AI assistant to compare vendors, employers or investment targets and it picks a shortlist. Nobody’s watching whether your company makes that shortlist, or why it doesn’t.

cards.title: The Sign
parts: You’d find out from a customer, a journalist or a screenshot — not from your own team. Nobody is systematically checking what ChatGPT, Gemini or Perplexity say about you until someone outside the company mentions it.
Why it matters
By the time it’s visible to you, it’s already been visible to everyone it’s going to reach. Early warning only works if someone's actually watching, continuously — not reacting after the fact.

cards.title: The Sign
parts: Nobody’s checked since the last model update. An answer that was fine last quarter can be wrong today, and nothing tells you unless you’re tracking it continuously.
Why it matters

It doesn’t wait for you to catch up. ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity retrain and re-index on their own schedules — so watching this has to be continuous, not a one-time check that ages out with the next release.

cards.title: The Sign
parts: Manual spot-checks catch a fraction of what’s actually being asked. Someone on the team occasionally types a question into ChatGPT — that’s not coverage, it’s a sample of one, on one platform, whenever someone remembers.
Why it matters

Coverage has to mean every platform, every day. ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Copilot and Google’s AI Overviews don’t answer the same way about the same company — missing one means missing exactly where the risk actually is.

AI monitoring is a young category because tracking what these models say about a company is a new problem, not because the risk is unproven. The pattern below is what happens when nobody's watching, and it will only get more common as more of what people read about a company comes from an AI answer instead of a search result. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework now treats exactly this class of exposure as a governance requirement, not an edge case.

questions.title: What is AI monitoring?

questions.title: What's the difference between this and AI Influence Services?
questions.answer: AI monitoring sits in RH Detection, and it's diagnostic: it tracks and scores what's being said, and alerts you. AI Influence Services is the Control-side program that acts on it — correcting the sources and signals the models draw from so the answer itself changes. Both currently sit in the same $5–25K/month range; the difference is watching versus fixing.

questions.title: Which AI platforms do you cover?
questions.answer: ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Microsoft Copilot and Google's AI Overviews, with coverage extended as new platforms gain meaningful usage among your customers, investors or candidates.

questions.title: Do you fix a wrong or outdated AI answer?
questions.answer: Not under this retainer. AI monitoring tracks, scores and alerts — it doesn't correct the sources a model draws from. When an answer needs active correction, we scope that as AI Influence Services, a separate workstream.

questions.title: How fast do I get alerted when something changes?
questions.answer: Depends on how each platform re-indexes or retrains — some shifts surface within days, others only at the next major model update. We track this per platform and alert on actual score movement, not a fixed reporting cycle.

questions.title: Is this confidential?
questions.answer: Yes. Every engagement runs under strict confidentiality terms, designed to be discreet by default — including work involving named executives.

questions.title: How is pricing structured?

questions.title: Does AI monitoring cover social platforms' AI features too?

questions.title: How does brand monitoring for AI results differ from regular search monitoring?
questions.answer: Regular search monitoring tracks where you rank in a list of blue links. AI results are different — there's no ranking, just one generated answer that either represents you accurately or doesn't. We track the answer itself, across every platform, and flag it the moment it turns wrong.

questions.title: What is brand reputation management?
questions.answer: Brand reputation management — or reputation management for business, if you're searching by outcome rather than category — is the ongoing practice of monitoring, protecting and shaping everything a company's market finds about it: search, reviews, media narrative, sentiment and AI-generated answers.It is the enterprise form of online reputation management, run with an owned narrative, a dedicated team and a measurement framework, rather than reacting to individual results as they appear. At Reputation House it is delivered as Strategic Information-Field Management, RH Control's full-program retainer.

questions.title: What is the difference between ORM and SERM?
questions.answer: SERM covers one surface: what ranks on Google, Bing and YouTube for your brand name. Online reputation management covers all of them, adding reviews, media narrative and AI answers. SERM is a workstream inside this program and also runs as a standalone retainer, as does the narrative and content layer on its own.

questions.title: What are the key strategies for effective reputation management?
questions.answer: A working reputation strategy has four parts, and a reputation management strategy that skips any one of them leaks. Continuous reputation monitoring, so you learn about a problem before your customers do. A content strategy that builds owned assets worth ranking, supported by search engine optimization rather than replaced by it. Structured review management services, so ratings reflect the actual customer base. And a crisis protocol agreed in advance, so the first hour of a bad day is not spent deciding who speaks. Proactive reputation management is cheaper than repair, consistently.

questions.title: How much do reputation management services cost?
questions.answer: Across the market the range runs from a few hundred dollars a month for a review-response tool to five figures a month for a fully managed enterprise program. This one is a monthly retainer, $10–50K/month, scoped to region, channels and the size of your information field rather than listed as a package. Single workstreams are cheaper on their own. Full tiers by region are on the pricing page, and a confidential audit confirms the exact quote.

questions.title: How long does this take to show results?
questions.answer: Monitoring starts immediately, with threat detection inside 24–48 hours. Measurable shifts typically appear in 8–12 weeks, with significant change in 3–6 months, depending on scope.

questions.title: Can you remove negative content or negative search results from Google?
questions.answer: Sometimes. Where content breaches a platform's policy, contains factual errors or infringes a legal right, negative content removal is possible and we pursue it. Where it does not, the honest answer is suppression: we build and rank stronger assets so the harmful result drops down the page. We do not promise to remove negative news articles that are lawful and accurate, and anyone who does is describing something we would not sign.

questions.title: How do you handle negative reviews and negative feedback?
questions.answer: By responding, not by hiding. Every negative review gets a reply written to be read by the next reader rather than by the complainant, since that is who it actually persuades. Underneath that, we track patterns across review sites and social media platforms: repeated customer review themes are usually a product signal, and passing that back is worth more than any individual response. Volume of positive reviews is then built the legitimate way, by asking satisfied customers at the right moment, never by buying them.

questions.title: How does AI change online reputation management?
questions.answer: It changes what counts as page one. Assistants answer directly instead of listing links, so a single stale source can become the whole answer, and there is no second page to correct it. On our side the same shift helps: AI-assisted analysis of brand mentions and online feedback classifies sentiment across languages far faster than a human team, which makes early detection realistic rather than aspirational. The optimization work itself stays human.

questions.title: How do you measure brand reputation?
questions.answer: Against a baseline set during the audit. The standing KPIs are share of positive and neutral results on page one, share of voice against named competitors, sentiment analysis across monitored online mentions, review ratings and volume by platform, and the accuracy of AI answers about your company. Brand mention monitoring runs continuously underneath all of it, so every number has a movement behind it rather than a snapshot.

questions.title: Do you guarantee specific rankings, removals or ratings?
questions.answer: No. We commit to compliant methods and transparent reporting on what moved and what didn't, not guaranteed removals, fake reviews or blackhat tactics.

questions.title: Is this the same as PR, and can you work alongside our in-house team?
questions.answer: It is not the same, and yes. Public relations shapes what publications say about you; this shapes what anyone finds afterwards, which includes coverage but also review platforms, forums, AI answers and your own online brand assets. Digital marketing drives demand; this work makes sure the person that demand sends to Google finds a positive reputation waiting. RH Control is built to run alongside in-house marketing, PR, communications and compliance teams as operational capacity, not as a replacement for the function.

questions.title: Which industries and regions do you cover?

questions.title: What should you look for in a reputation management company?
questions.answer: Three things separate a reputation management agency worth retaining from one that is not. First, method transparency: a reputation management firm that names what it will actually do, and refuses fake reviews and blackhat SEO in writing. Second, coverage: whether it can act on search, reviews, media and AI answers, or only on one of them. Third, accountability: a named strategist, agreed KPIs and reporting tied to business outcomes rather than impressions. sections.title: What is Search Engine Reputation Management?
body: When customers, partners, or investors search for your company, the first page of Google forms their first impression — before any conversation happens. Negative articles, outdated stories, fake reviews, or competitor attacks can all appear there, and every decision-maker who Googles your brand sees this content first.
aside: Search Engine Reputation Management — also called SEO reputation management or reputation management SEO — is the practice of taking control over what Google shows about your brand. We suppress negative content, push it off the first page through positive and authoritative material, and maintain this control over time — so your search results support your business, not undermine it.

cards.title: Take control of harmful content

The brand's search presence shifted from a liability to a neutral, accurate reflection of the company. Inbound lead quality improved. The client transitioned to an ongoing management engagement to ensure the results held over time.

Within weeks, the company's search results shifted from a wall of crisis coverage to a balanced picture that included the company's own perspective and subsequent actions. The autocomplete suggestions normalized. The company retained the engagement for ongoing monitoring.

We work with the same ranking signals Google actually uses, which is why this approach holds long-term.

SERM is about controlling everything that appears when someone searches for your brand — your website, third-party articles, business profiles, reviews, news mentions, social platforms, AI search results.SEO focuses on traffic. SERM focuses on perception. The skills overlap, but the goals are different. SERM combines content strategy, technical SEO, digital PR, and ongoing monitoring to shape what shows up on page one of search results.

sections.title: Types Of Brand Positioning Strategies We Actually Work Inside
body:
There is no shortage of frameworks. In practice most companies already sit inside one of a few types of brand positioning, and the useful question is whether the footprint supports it and whether it differentiates anything. Most positioning strategies fail on evidence, not on wording.

A brand promise, a brand personality, a positioning statement: the internal work is usually done. What is missing is proof that any of it survived contact with a journalist, a forum thread or an AI summary.

cards.title: Quality-based positioning
parts: Works when the proof is public. Reviews, retention, independent coverage. It fails quietly when the claim runs ahead of the evidence, and sentiment is usually where that gap surfaces first.

cards.title: Customer service positioning
parts: The easiest position to claim and the hardest to hold, because every customer with a keyboard is a witness. We track it where it actually gets decided: forums, video, support threads.

cards.title: Competitor-led positioning
parts: Sometimes the fastest way to differentiate your brand is to name what you are not. It also hands a competitor the frame, so we use it only where the market has already made the comparison for you.

cards.title: Value and price positioning
parts: A value proposition leaning on price needs the rest of the story to carry weight,or the brand turns into a line item. Gaps in the market are usually narrower here than a pitch deck suggests.

sections.title: Perception over positioning

A brand storytelling strategy is the enjoyable part to write; checking whether the story resonated outside your own marketing materials is the part that gets skipped. sections.title: What You should Know of Brand Positioning

cards.title: What Is Brand Positioning? What It Actually Means
parts: Brand positioning is the place a company occupies in someone else's head relative to the alternatives — the brand promise as it's actually received, not the sentence in the deck the company would say out loud if prompted. When the two match, the positioning works; usually they do not, and the gap is measurable.

cards.title: Why Is Brand Positioning Important? Why It Matters for a Business
parts: Because it decides how much explaining every deal needs. Weak positioning shows up as longer sales cycles, higher acquisition cost and investors filling in the blanks themselves. It behaves like a revenue input long before anyone treats it as one. What people remember your brand for also decides how far a brand marketing budget goes: buyers who already place the product or brand correctly need a lot less convincing.

cards.title: The 3 C’s and 4 C’s of Brand Positioning
parts: The 3 C's — company, customer, competitor — are a sanity check on whether a claim is true, wanted and still unclaimed. The 4 C's add channel or context, depending on who is teaching it. Useful as a filter, useless as a deliverable: neither framework tells you what the market currently believes.

cards.title: How to Create a Brand Positioning Strategy When One Already Exists
parts: Audit what is being said now, isolate the themes worth keeping, decide what needs redirecting, then place content and outreach until the corrected version outweighs the old one. That order matters. Most failed attempts start at the writing and never check the baseline.

cards.title: How a Perceptual Map (Positioning Map) Is Used in Brand Strategy
parts: A perceptual map (also called a positioning map) is good for one thing: showing leadership that two competitors already own the axis they wanted. It is a discussion tool, not evidence, so we plot ours against live mention and sentiment data rather than opinion from the room.

cards.title: How to Measure Brand Positioning: Effectiveness Metrics That Matter
parts: Share of voice and other brand awareness metrics: the share of mentions carrying the intended theme, the sentiment attached to each theme, how often the competing framing shows up, and what search and AI assistants answer when asked about the company. Reported weekly and compared against the baseline taken at the audit — not once a quarter, when it is already someone else's question.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions

questions.title: What is a brand positioning statement?
questions.answer: A brand positioning statement is the internal sentence that describes where a brand sits relative to alternatives — for whom, against what, and why it's the better choice. The gap we work on isn't writing that sentence; it's making sure the market's actual perception matches it.

questions.title: What is Brand Reputation & Narrative Management?
questions.answer: The RH Control retainer that tracks and actively corrects an existing brand positioning strategy that has gone blurry, mixed or lost to a competitor's framing — narrative and tone tracking, plus social listening. A dedicated narrative strategist and content team run it, not a one-off messaging deck.

questions.title: What's the difference between this and Reputation Building & Market Entry?
questions.answer: Reputation Building & Market Entry is where we create a brand positioning strategy from zero, for a new target market or brand with almost no existing footprint. Brand Reputation & Narrative Management is the opposite situation — an existing narrative that's gone blurry, mixed or lost to a competitor's version of the story. If the footprint doesn't exist yet, that's the other program; if it exists but isn't working, it's this one.

questions.title: Does the positioning statement need a reason to believe?
questions.answer: Yes — a positioning statement without a reason to believe is just a claim. We test the reason to believe against live mention and sentiment data before it goes into anything public, not just against what sounds good internally.

questions.title: How long until we see results?
questions.answer: Narrative and tone shifts typically become measurable within 6–10 weeks. A consistently dominant narrative across mentions, media and AI answers usually takes 3–6 months, depending on how diluted the current positioning is, and how much brand recall the competing version has already built.

questions.title: Is this confidential?
questions.answer: Yes. Every engagement runs under strict confidentiality — brand positioning plans are commercially sensitive by nature, and we treat them that way from the first contact.

questions.title: Do you replace our in-house communications team?
questions.answer: No. We work alongside the in-house communications, marketing or IR team as narrative capacity — not a replacement for the function.

questions.title: Do you guarantee a specific sentiment score or media pickup?
questions.answer: No. We commit to compliant methods and transparent reporting on what actually shifted — not guaranteed sentiment numbers, planted coverage or manufactured narratives.

questions.title: Do you offer one-off brand positioning consulting?
questions.answer: No — this runs as an ongoing retainer, not a single consulting engagement. A one-time positioning workshop can hand you a new statement; it can't track whether the market adopted it six months later. That's the part we're built for.

An out-of-context clip of an executive began circulating with a coordinated hashtag push, echoing the shape of prior category boycotts — negative mentions rose 6x within 24 hours.

cards.title: Starbucks Korea
cards.subtitle: Consumer · Culturally-insensitive campaign, uncontained
before: What happened

A “Tank Day” promotion referencing military imagery landed on the anniversary of the 1980 Gwangju massacre. By week 3 the CEO was dismissed; by week 4 the parent company's chairman issued a public apology; by week 5 government ministries began cancelling contracts; by week 6 every store closed nationwide for mandatory history training, with no timeline for a sales recovery.
after: Each week without a coordinated response escalated the story to a new audience — customers, then the corporate parent, then government stakeholders, then employees. What could have been contained in the first 72 hours instead spent six weeks compounding into a systemic crisis with no single fix.
cards.source: The Guardian, 16 Jun 2026

sections.title: Brand Protection & Community Safety: Frequently Asked Questions

questions.title: What is Brand Protection & Community Safety Solution?
questions.answer: An RH Defence retainer that watches community-heavy platforms — Reddit, X, forums, review sites — for coordinated attacks, brigading and brand impersonation, and puts a dedicated response team on a coordinated wave before it becomes a crisis.

questions.title: How is this different from Crisis Management?
questions.answer: Crisis Management is for an active, already-unfolding crisis — project priced with a crisis surcharge, from $50–100K+/month during the active phase. Brand Protection & Community Safety is the ongoing retainer that detects and contains coordinated attacks before it reaches that point, and hands off to Crisis Management if one does.

questions.title: How is this different from Reputation Repair & Negative Suppression?
questions.answer: Reputation Repair is about pushing down already-published damaging search or media content under active legal pressure. Brand Protection & Community Safety is about detecting and responding to coordinated UGC attacks, brigading and impersonation as they're forming — a different threat and a different workstream.

questions.title: How fast does detection actually happen?
questions.answer: Monitoring is live from launch. Coordinated posting patterns and impersonation attempts are typically flagged within hours of forming, not after they've picked up traction.

questions.title: What should I do if someone is impersonating my company online?
questions.answer: Document the fake accounts, pages or sites and don't engage with them. Brand impersonation protection at scale works the same way, only faster: the SCAN module flags impersonation attempts as they form, and once one is confirmed our response team files the specific report each platform requires and tracks it through to resolution. Takedown timing depends on each platform's own process.

questions.title: What is the difference between brand protection and reputation management?
questions.answer: Brand reputation protection, as we run it, means watching for organized threats to your brand as they form — coordinated attacks, brigading, impersonation — and acting on them. Reputation management works on the wider information field: search results, reviews, media narrative and AI answers. If you need those managed together as one program, that's the RH Control solutions group.

questions.title: What is brandjacking?
questions.answer: Brandjacking is when someone imitates or takes over a brand's identity online — fake accounts, spoofed pages or lookalike sites — to collect followers, messages or money from people who think they're dealing with the brand. It is one of the coordinated-attack patterns this solution watches for.

questions.title: Does the platform use AI to detect coordinated attacks?
questions.answer: Yes. Detection combines machine-learning and AI models with analyst review: every mention is scored for coordination signals — shared phrasing, account-creation timing, posting velocity — and the response team acts on what the scoring flags.

questions.title: Is this confidential?
questions.answer: Yes. Every engagement runs under strict confidentiality terms, designed to be discreet by default.

questions.title: Do you replace our in-house community or social team?
questions.answer: No. Brand Protection & Community Safety runs alongside your existing community and social team, escalating coordinated activity that needs a response — not replacing day-to-day community management.

questions.title: Do you guarantee an attack won't happen, or that fake accounts get removed?
questions.answer: No. We can't guarantee an attack never starts, and takedown timing for impersonation accounts depends on each platform's own process. We commit to early detection, fast reporting and an active response — not guaranteed prevention or removal timelines.

questions.title: What is the cost of online brand protection services?
questions.answer: A monthly retainer, $5–25K/month, depending on the platforms covered and region. Full tiers are on the pricing page, or a confidential audit confirms the exact quote.

questions.title: What are media relations services?
questions.answer: Media relations services place a company's story in the business and trade press: feature articles, expert commentary, company profiles and interviews. Business media presence is the result: the body of coverage about your business in industry publications, built so it holds up when someone checks your company name and adds credibility your company cannot claim for itself. It is not a single press release or a launch announcement. It is the record a client or a partner finds months later, and the part of your business reputation that verifies what your company says about itself.

questions.title: How is a media relations agency different from a PR agency?
questions.answer: A media relations agency or PR agency is usually measured in visibility: placements, followers, speaking slots. This solution is measured in what the record shows under your company's name afterwards — whether the coverage ranks, whether it is consistent with everything else public about your company, and whether it holds up under a due-diligence check. Placement is the method here, not the outcome.

questions.title: Is this a PR agency for B2B companies?

questions.title: What formats do you place?
questions.answer: Feature articles and contributed op-eds, expert commentary and quotes in journalists' stories, company profiles and interviews, and contributed pieces in trade and industry press. The format follows the outlet and the audience, not a template. What we don't do is send the same text everywhere and call it coverage. This is earned media, not advertising: editors decide what runs. If you know this work as thought leadership services, this is its placement half, measured by what the record shows rather than by impressions.

questions.title: Do you write the content, or does our team?
questions.answer: We draft, your company approves, and nothing goes out without sign-off. Most companies have the expertise and no time to write it; the work is turning what your team already knows into something an editor will publish. The ideas and the position have to be your company's — we don't invent a point of view it doesn't hold.

questions.title: Do you guarantee placement in a specific publication?

We commit to a realistic media plan based on what your category actually publishes, compliant methods, and transparent reporting on what ran and what it did.
